By the middle of July the sunflowers in Plot 10 stood taller than the tool shed, and by the first of August Mrs. Ruiz had written to the garden committee. Nia, who was thirteen and had become the committee's secretary because she was the only member who liked taking notes, read the letter aloud at the Tuesday meeting under the maple tree.

Mr. Haddad's sunflowers, the letter said, had been planted in a row along the west side of her plot, just across the narrow path that divided his plot from hers, and they were taking her afternoon sun. Her tomatoes had been green for three weeks. The whole plot, she wrote, now spent the afternoon in shade.

Mr. Haddad said it was a few leaves at most. He had planted the sunflowers for the goldfinches, which would come for the seeds in September, and the committee had approved his planting list in April.

Mrs. Ruiz said the committee had approved sunflowers, not a wall. Mr. Haddad said that a wall would at least stand still in the wind. They went on like this until Mr. Pruitt, the chair, said the matter would wait a week, and everyone folded their chairs.

On Saturday Nia came to the garden at noon with a bundle of bamboo stakes, a marker, and her mother's watch. At the top of each hour she found the edge of the sunflowers' shadow, pushed a stake into the soil where it lay, and wrote the hour on the stake. At noon the shadow stayed inside Plot 10. At two it reached the path. At three the stake went in beside the first row of tomatoes, and at five beside the second. The six o'clock stake stood at the edge of the third row. The fourth row was still in full sunlight when she went home for dinner.

At the next meeting she asked everyone to walk over to the two plots instead of sitting down. Seven stakes stood in a ragged line, running from the foot of the sunflowers out across the path and into the tomatoes, and Nia read the hour written on each one.

Mrs. Ruiz looked at the line for a long time. Then she said that her two near rows lost the sun after three, and that her far rows kept it until evening. Mr. Haddad looked at the five o'clock stake standing among her tomato vines and said that was more than a few leaves.

Next spring, he said, he would plant his sunflowers at the north end of his plot, beside the gravel walk, where their shadows would fall mostly on the walk. Mrs. Ruiz said she might put lettuce in her two near rows, since lettuce could stand a little afternoon shade.

Nia wrote it all into the minutes. She left the stakes where they were, and nobody pulled them up.

In September the goldfinches came, as Mr. Haddad had said they would, hanging upside down from the heavy flower heads. Mrs. Ruiz was the one who saw them first, and she called across the path for him to come and look.

In the coldest week the window by my bed
grew ferns overnight, white ones,
feathered and branching, laid up the glass
as if someone had pressed them there to dry.

Our house was old. The panes were single,
and the heat from the kitchen stove
gave out halfway up the stairs, so that my breath
hung in the room like a small cloud I could watch.

I would lie under three blankets and study them:
the long stems climbing from the bottom of the pane,
the little fronds that met in the middle
and stopped, as though they had agreed to.

Then I would press my thumb against the glass
and hold it there, counting, while the cold went up my arm,
until a round clear hole opened
and the yard came through it, small and bright.

Through that hole I saw the whole of the morning:
the shed roof heaped, the fence posts capped,
my father's tracks going out to the woodpile
and the same tracks coming back, deeper.

By noon the sun had reached that side of the house,
and the ferns let go from the top down,
going gray, then to water, then to a few
bright beads that ran and left the glass plain.

And every night they grew back, closing my hole,
so that each morning I had to make it again,
the same thumb, the same count, the same small yard
coming back to me out of the white.

I live now in a house with double panes.
The glass stays clear all winter,
which is better, everyone tells me, and it is.
Some mornings I still put my thumb to it, and wait.

The summer I was sixteen I worked the paint counter at Gorski's Hardware, a narrow store with creaking floors and a bell over the door. The store had a machine that shook a can of paint for three minutes, but nothing that could read a color. When customers wanted to match an old color, they brought in a chip of it, and someone at the counter matched it by eye.

That someone was usually Dolores, who had worked the counter for twenty-six years. She taught me the first rule on my first morning. Colorant goes into the white base a few drops at a time, she said, because you can always put in more. Once it is in, it stays in.

For the first two weeks I mostly watched. I noticed that every match she made went to the front window before the can went into the shaker, even on gray days, even with customers waiting, and I took it for a habit left over from some older store. It seemed like a lot of walking for a color that already looked right. Then one morning a man came in with a curl of green paint he had peeled from a porch shutter, and Dolores was at lunch.

I worked at that green for most of an hour. I added yellow, then a drop of black, then more yellow, smearing a dab of each try on a card and holding it beside the chip under the long lights over the counter. At last the two greens were the same. I could see no line where one ended and the other began. I mixed his quart, hammered on the lid, and felt like a professional.

He was back the next afternoon with the quart and the shutter itself, painted half with my green and half still with the old. On the porch, he said, the new half looked blue. I held the shutter up under the long lights, and the two halves looked identical. Then Dolores carried it to the front window and set it in the sun, and there it was: a cool stripe beside a warmer one.

Dolores did not scold me. She mixed a fresh quart, adding colorant a drop at a time, and before it went into the shaker she carried the can and the chip to the window twice to compare them in the daylight.

"You matched it for the counter," she said. "He has to live with it on a porch."

By August I was carrying cans to the window myself. I learned that a match could hold under one light and come apart under another, and that the light that counted was wherever the paint would end up: a kitchen, a bedroom facing north, a porch in the afternoon. I learned to ask customers where the paint was going before I opened the base.

I have not mixed paint in years. But I still catch myself, holding up a shirt in a store, walking it over to the door to see what color it will be outside.

In the dry summer of 1854, the Corran Canal nearly ran out of water at its highest point. From the river at Pellam the canal climbed through eleven locks to a summit level two miles long, then dropped through nine more toward the lake. The summit level was fed by Bracket Pond, a reservoir in the hills, and by the third week of July the pond had fallen four feet below its usual mark.

Every boat that crossed the summit cost it water. To raise a boat into the summit level, a keeper filled the lock chamber with water let in from above, and once that water had passed into the chamber it was gone from the summit for good.

The company's directors met in Pellam to discuss closing the canal until the autumn rains. The town's merchants, who shipped flour east by water and received coal and salt the same way, sent a petition asking them to wait.

The proposal that kept the canal open came from Ezra Tolland, keeper of Lock 12 at the western end of the summit. Tolland had noticed something in his own log. When a boat coming up was followed by a boat going down, the chamber was already full when the second boat arrived, and he had only to let the water out beneath it. Two boats had cost the summit one filling. But when two boats came up one after another, he had to empty the chamber between them and fill it again, and two boats cost two fillings.

His proposal, which boatmen soon called the turn rule, was that a boat arriving at a summit lock should wait until a boat came from the other direction, so that the two could pass in turn. To keep a boat from being held all day, the wait was limited to four hours. The directors adopted the rule for both summit locks on July 28.

The boatmen hated it. Captains paid by the trip lost half a day at a time tied up below Lock 12, and one of them, Silas Varney, threatened to take the company to court.

But the pond's fall slowed. By the company's records, taken each morning at a marked post on the shore of the reservoir, it dropped at a little more than half its earlier rate, and the canal stayed open until rain came in the second week of September. Pellam's mills shipped their flour that autumn as usual.

The turn rule was put into force in every dry summer after that, and a painted board stating it hung beside Lock 12 until the canal closed in 1889, eighteen years after the railroad reached Pellam. The board is now in the town hall. Tolland's name is not on it.

In the dry summer of 1854, the Corran Canal nearly ran out of water at its highest point. From the river at Pellam the canal climbed through eleven locks to a summit level two miles long, then dropped through nine more toward the lake. The summit level was fed by Bracket Pond, a reservoir in the hills, and by the third week of July the pond had fallen four feet below its usual mark.

Every boat that crossed the summit cost it water. To raise a boat into the summit level, a keeper filled the lock chamber with water let in from above, and once that water had passed into the chamber it was gone from the summit for good.

The company's directors met in Pellam to discuss closing the canal until the autumn rains. The town's merchants, who shipped flour east by water and received coal and salt the same way, sent a petition asking them to wait.

The proposal that kept the canal open came from Ezra Tolland, keeper of Lock 12 at the western end of the summit. Tolland had noticed something in his own log. When a boat coming up was followed by a boat going down, the chamber was already full when the second boat arrived, and he had only to let the water out beneath it. Two boats had cost the summit one filling. But when two boats came up one after another, he had to empty the chamber between them and fill it again, and two boats cost two fillings.

His proposal, which boatmen soon called the turn rule, was that a boat arriving at a summit lock should wait until a boat came from the other direction, so that the two could pass in turn. To keep a boat from being held all day, the wait was limited to four hours. The directors adopted the rule for both summit locks on July 28.

The boatmen hated it. Captains paid by the trip lost half a day at a time tied up below Lock 12, and one of them, Silas Varney, threatened to take the company to court.

But the pond's fall slowed. By the company's records, taken each morning at a marked post on the shore of the reservoir, it dropped at a little more than half its earlier rate, and the canal stayed open until rain came in the second week of September. Pellam's mills shipped their flour that autumn as usual.

The turn rule was put into force in every dry summer after that, and a painted board stating it hung beside Lock 12 until the canal closed in 1889, eighteen years after the railroad reached Pellam. The board is now in the town hall. Tolland's name is not on it.

item.passage:
A loggerhead sea turtle begins life buried in sand. After about two months in the nest, the hatchlings dig their way up together, usually at night, and scramble for the water. Their first guide is light. On a natural beach, the open horizon over the sea is brighter than the land behind them, with its dunes and plants, and the hatchlings crawl toward the brighter side. Lights from buildings and roads can draw them the wrong way, which is why many beach towns where turtles nest now ask residents to keep their lights low in summer.

Once in the water, the hatchlings swim into the waves. Near shore, waves generally travel toward the beach, so swimming against them carries a turtle out to sea. But waves are a useful guide only for the first few miles. Hatchlings from the beaches of Florida must find their way into the North Atlantic gyre, a vast loop of currents that circles the ocean, and stay in it for years as they grow. Drifting out of it to the north can carry a young turtle into water cold enough to kill it.

How does a turtle the size of a cookie keep to a current thousands of miles around? Part of the answer appears to be magnetism. The earth's magnetic field differs from place to place in two ways an animal could in principle detect: its strength, and the angle at which its lines meet the surface, which is nearly flat near the equator and steep near the poles. Together these give many locations a kind of magnetic signature.

In a series of experiments, researchers placed hatchlings in a round pool surrounded by large coils of wire. By running current through the coils, they could expose the turtles to a field like that of a distant place, such as a point near the gyre's eastern edge off Portugal, while the turtles never left the laboratory. The hatchlings, held in light harnesses so that their swimming direction could be recorded, tended to swim in whichever direction would, in the real ocean, have kept them inside the gyre.

The same sense may guide them home. Female loggerheads return to nest on or near the beach where they hatched, often after decades at sea, and some researchers have proposed that a hatchling records the magnetic signature of its home beach and later seeks it out. One study of nesting records along the Florida coast found that where the slowly drifting field made neighboring stretches of shore more alike, nests became more crowded, as that idea would predict. The idea remains unproven, but it fits the evidence so far.

What no one has yet found is the sense organ itself. Animals as different as turtles, birds and salmon respond to magnetic fields, yet the cells that detect the field have proved remarkably hard to locate, which makes the question all the more tantalizing. For now, a newly hatched loggerhead carries a map that scientists can read only by watching where it swims.

A loggerhead sea turtle begins life buried in sand. After about two months in the nest, the hatchlings dig their way up together, usually at night, and scramble for the water. Lights from buildings and roads can draw them the wrong way, which is why many beach towns where turtles nest now ask residents to keep their lights low in summer.

Once in the water, the hatchlings swim into the waves. Near shore, waves generally travel toward the beach, so swimming against them carries a turtle out to sea. But waves are a useful guide only for the first few miles. Hatchlings from the beaches of Florida must find their way into the North Atlantic gyre, a vast loop of currents that circles the ocean, and stay in it for years as they grow. Drifting out of it to the north can carry a young turtle into water cold enough to kill it.

How does a turtle the size of a cookie keep to a current thousands of miles around? Part of the answer appears to be magnetism. The earth's magnetic field differs from place to place in two ways an animal could in principle detect: its strength, and the angle at which its lines meet the surface, which is nearly flat near the equator and steep near the poles. Together these give many locations a kind of magnetic signature.

In a series of experiments, researchers placed hatchlings in a round pool surrounded by large coils of wire. By running current through the coils, they could expose the turtles to a field like that of a distant place, such as a point near the gyre's eastern edge off Portugal, while the turtles never left the laboratory. The hatchlings, held in light harnesses so that their swimming direction could be recorded, tended to swim in whichever direction would, in the real ocean, have kept them inside the gyre.

The same sense may guide them home. Female loggerheads return to nest on or near the beach where they hatched, often after decades at sea, and some researchers have proposed that a hatchling records the magnetic signature of its home beach and later seeks it out. One study of nesting records along the Florida coast found that where the slowly drifting field made neighboring stretches of shore more alike, nests became more crowded, as that idea would predict. The idea remains unproven, but it fits the evidence so far.

What no one has yet found is the sense organ itself. Animals as different as turtles, birds and salmon respond to magnetic fields, yet the cells that detect the field have proved remarkably hard to locate, which makes the question all the more tantalizing. For now, a newly hatched loggerhead carries a map that scientists can read only by watching where it swims.
